info.bio:
INXS es una banda de Rock y New Wave de Australia. Su nombre es el acrónimo de In excess (en exceso). Fue formada el 16 de agosto de 1977 en Sydney.

Historia

En la escuela Preparatoria, el cantante Michael Hutchence conoció al teclista y guitarrista Andrew Farriss, en medio de una pelea en la que Mike estaba metido. Andrew logró ayudarlo y desde entonces fueron grandes amigos. Por esos años decidieron formar una banda junto al bajista Garry Gary Beers.

scenes.name: Pop de Australia y Nueva Zelanda
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Australia aporta las elegías neorrománticas de los Go-Betweens, las microsinfonías de The Church, Hunters And Collectors, Midnight Oil, Men At Work, Triffids e INXS. Nueva Zelanda cría una generación de antihéroes que no tiene nada que ver con la ola británica comercial y crea el género de los noventa: el «lo-fi pop». The Clean (como si los Buzzcocks versionaran a Syd Barrett y a la Velvet), Tall Dwarfs, Chills, Bats, This Kind Of Punishment, Jean Paul Sartre Experience, Scorched Earth Policy, Able Tasmans, Verlaines y la figura de Peter Jefferies.

podcast.title: Name Change (1979)
podcast.body: The group transitioned from "The Farriss Brothers" to "InXS" in 1979. "In 1979, the group changed their name. They became known as in excess."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: First International Deal (1982)
podcast.body: In 1982, InXS secured their first international record deal, marking a significant step toward global recognition. "The Big Break came in 1982 when in excess signed their first international deal."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Peak Popularity (1987-1991)
podcast.body: Between 1987 and 1991, InXS achieved massive global success, with millions in album sales, widespread music and video presence, and hugely profitable concert tours. A show in Mexico City grossed over $1 million, a Wembley Stadium concert in London grossed over $3 million, and over 100,000 fans attended a show in Rio de Janeiro. Some critics even considered U2 their only rivals worldwide. "Between 1987 and 1991, Inexess was everywhere."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Health Impact of Copenhagen Altercation (1992)
podcast.body: Following an altercation with a taxi driver in Copenhagen in 1992, Michael Hutchence suffered a fractured skull, after which he was reportedly "not quite the same." "Michael wasn't quite the same after an altercation with a taxi driver in Copenhagen in 1992 that resulted in him suffering a fractured skull."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 20th Anniversary TV Special (1997)
podcast.body: In November and December 1997, InXS was in Sydney filming a TV special for Australian television to commemorate their 20th anniversary, coinciding with local performance dates. "In excess was back home in Sydney, filming a TV special for Australian TV. Everybody was pumped up for this documentary commemorating the 20th anniversary of In Excess, which coincided with some dates at home in November and December."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death (November 22–23, 1997) – Ritz Carlton Sydney, Belt, No Suicide Note; Coroner: Consistent with Auto-Erotic Asphyxiation
podcast.body: The night before Michael Hutchence's death began normally: a dinner with his father and stepmother at a restaurant called the Flapper of India, where he seemed fine. He returned to room 524 at the Ritz Carlton Double Bay, Sydney. Ex-girlfriend Kim Wilson (inspiration for "Suicide Blonde") came to the hotel with her boyfriend; they drank daiquiris, champagne, and beer in the bar before going to Hutchence's room. They left around 4am. Over the following hours, Hutchence made multiple calls but reached only answering machines. Early that morning he went downstairs looking disheveled to mail some letters — the last time anyone saw him alive. A maid found his body around noon on Saturday, November 23. He appeared to have gone into a violent rage — prescription pills scattered across the room, a broken hand from hitting the wall, facial cuts, furniture thrown — before fastening a leather belt to the bathroom door and hanging himself. There was no suicide note. The official coroner's verdict was death consistent with auto-erotic asphyxiation, a practice that kills an estimated 500 to 1,000 people per year worldwide. Hutchence had acknowledged in a late interview trying to achieve "the ultimate sexual high," and his mother confirmed he had spent time with sadomasochists in the preceding months. "The coroner says is consistent with auto-erotic asphyxiation, a death by misadventure."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Decline in Late 1990s and 20th Anniversary Special (1997)
podcast.body: By the late 1990s, the "best days" of INXS were considered to be behind them, although they remained a profitable concern. On November 22, 1997, the band was in Sydney, Australia, working on a TV special to commemorate their 20th anniversary. "By the late 90s, the best days of InXS were behind them, but they were still very much a profitable concern."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Last Public Sightings and Communications (November 1997)
podcast.body: On the night of Friday, November 21, 1997, Michael Hutchence had an Indian dinner with his father and stepmother, appearing to have a good time despite his father's unease. He returned to Room 524 at the Ritz Carlton Hotel in Sydney around 10:30 PM, joking with girls in the elevator. He then went on a "last bender," making calls to former girlfriends Kim Wilson (who visited with her current boyfriend until 4 AM) and Michelle Bennett (who rushed to the hotel after a worried call but found no answer). He also had two calls with Bob Geldof around 5 AM about a court injunction, including a loud 20-minute argument, and a desperate-sounding call with Paula Yates at 5:38 AM. His last sighting was asking a front desk clerk to mail two letters—one to Paula and one to a friend in Hong Kong. "Sometime after that, Michael went down to the front desk and asked the clerk to mail two letters, one to Paula and the other to a friend in Hong Kong. That was the last time anyone saw him alive."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Michael Hutchins' Death (November 1997)
podcast.body: Michael Hutchins, identified as the singer for "in excess," died in November 1997 by hanging. "Michael Hutchins, singer, in excess, death by hanging for some reason, November 1997."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New Record Deal and Album (1997)
podcast.body: At the start of 1997, InXS secured a new record deal and had an album in production, signaling their intent for a professional "fresh start." "By the beginning of 1997, in excess had a new record deal and a new album on the way. Professionally, the group was looking for a fresh start."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Relationship Turmoil and Self-Medication (November 1997)
podcast.body: Michael Hutchence was experiencing intense personal turmoil due to his relationship with UK TV presenter Paula Yates, the ex-wife of Bob Geldof, especially concerning a dispute over children. He was described as not being in a good place and was self-medicating with drugs, including heroin, which he and Paula were both using. "The turmoil with Paula and Bob was peaking over children. She was expecting. He was self-medicating."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Suicide (November 1997)
podcast.body: Between 9:55 AM and 10:30 AM on Saturday, November 22, 1997, Michael Hutchence, depressed, drunk, and sleep-deprived, entered a violent rage, throwing furniture, punching a wall, breaking his hand, and scattering five different prescription pills. He then hanged himself with a leather snakeskin belt from a doorknob in his hotel room. A housekeeper discovered his body at 11:50 AM. No suicide note was found. "depressed, drunk, and sleep deprived, Michael had gone into a violent rage, throwing furniture around, breaking his hand, punching a wall, and scattering five different prescription pills all over the place. Sometime between 955 AM and 1030 AM, he hanged himself with a leather snake skin belt from a doorknob."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Album Sales
podcast.body: The band sold close to 80 million albums, establishing them as the second biggest Australian success story, after AC/DC. "His band had sold somewhere near 80 million albums, putting them second only to, who, ACDC I guess, in terms of Australian success stories."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Australian Pub Circuit Development
podcast.body: The band honed their skills by playing at least 300 shows a year on the demanding Australian pub circuit, including mining towns and sheep stations, developing a distinctive "funky swagger." "It excess learned their chops the hard way on the grueling Australian pub circuit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Name Evolution
podcast.body: The group initially performed as The Farriss Brothers. When the Farriss family moved to Perth, the other band members stayed together under the name The Vegetables. By 1979, everyone reunited in Sydney and began performing as INXS, adopting a name aligned with the trend of "license plate names" popular at the time. "This became the Ferris brothers, and when the Ferris family moved to Perth, the other guys of the band stuck together under the name, the vegetables. But then everybody was back together in Sydney by 1979, where they started performing under the name in excess."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brief Christian Rock Endeavor
podcast.body: Early in their career, INXS briefly entertained the idea of breaking into the Christian rock market, an attempt that reportedly lasted "about a minute." "and originally the idea was to try to break into the Christian rock market, which lasted about a minute."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Bruce Fairbairn
podcast.body: Bruce Fairbairn produced mega-platinum albums for INXS throughout the 1980s and 1990s. "Throughout the 80s and 90s, he produced mega platinum albums for Erasmith and ACDC and Bon Jovi and Inaccess and Kiss and Leverboy and Poison, The Scorpions and Van Halen and a ton of others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Confirmed Imperiality
podcast.body: The Australian band INXS confirmed their imperial status with five or more top ten hits between 1986 and 1987, including four from their 1987 album "Kick." This period showed they were big enough to score with singles that did not even echo their original sound. "Their imperiality was confirmed. In excess was now big enough to score with singles that didn't even echo their original sound."

podcast.title: Decline in Best Years
podcast.body: By November 1997, the peak years of INXS seemed to be in the past, coinciding with Michael Hutchence's growing personal problems. "The best years of Inexcess seemed to have been in the rearview mirror by this time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Band Mergers
podcast.body: Andrew Farriss started in a high school band called Dr. Dolphin, later convincing Michael Hutchence to join. In 1977, Andrew's older brother Tim suggested merging Dr. Dolphin members (including Michael and Gary Beers) with a group called Guinness, which was named after a dog. This combined group initially became The Farriss Brothers. "The group started with Andrew Ferris. He was in a high school band called Dr. Dolphin, and somehow managed to convince a classmate named Michael Hutchins to join up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early International vs. Domestic Success
podcast.body: By summer 1983, InXS was drawing crowds of 14,000 people in Australia, showcasing their domestic popularity. However, their first American performance in San Diego in March 1983, was attended by only 24 people, highlighting the disparity in their early international reach. "Their first American performance, which was the show in San Diego in March 1983, was in front of 24 people."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fractured Band and Dimmed Career (Mid-1990s)
podcast.body: The band's career began to dim and fracture by the mid-1990s, heavily influenced by the erratic and aggressive behavior of their frontman Michael Hutchence, which was a direct result of an irreversible brain injury he sustained in 1992, and further exacerbated by his messy public breakup with Paula Yates. "in excess fractured, and their career dimmed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: John Hughes Film Exposure (1980s)
podcast.body: INXS's music was heavily mined for the soundtracks of John Hughes' 1980s films. These carefully curated soundtracks were instrumental in exposing numerous North American audiences to various alternative rock acts, especially those from the UK. "So many people learned of bands like The Specials and Spandovalet and Billy Idle and General Public and Wang Chung and Yellow and New Order and the Psychedelic Furs and the Smiths and Echo and the Bunyman, Susanne Vagan in excess the Jesus and Mary chain, Flesh for Luluo and so many others from those soundtrack albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Kick Album Initial Rejection
podcast.body: After recording *Kick*, InXS's record company in New York rejected it, deeming it "too funky, too dancing," and offered a million dollars for the band to start over. However, their manager bypassed the label by releasing it through college and alternative radio, leading to immediate success. "They took one listen and rejected it. Ah, too funky, too dancing, they said, look, here's a million dollars. Go back to Australia, start again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Michael Hutchence's Death and Band's End
podcast.body: Michael Hutchence's apparent accidental suicide in a Sydney hotel room in November 1997 marked a significant turning point for the band. Despite several attempts to continue with different singers, the public remained indifferent, leading to the band officially calling it quits. "and of course the apparent accidental suicide of Michael Hutchins in that Sydney hotel room in November of 1997. There were several attempts to keep going with a different singer, but the public has pretty much been indifferent to everything, so the band has officially called it quits."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Opening for Major Acts
podcast.body: InXS toured extensively, frequently serving as an opening act for prominent bands such as The Go-Go's, The Kinks, and Hall & Oates. "The band was on the road almost constantly, usually opening for someone like the Go-Go's or the Kinks or Holland Oats."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Hutchence Continuation
podcast.body: After Michael Hutchence's death, the band took a year-long hiatus before continuing with guest singers. They later participated in the reality TV series *Rock Star*, where Canadian singer JD Fortune was chosen as their new frontman. Fortune sang on one album, was fired, but then rehired a few years later. "In excess, tried to continue after taking a year off after Michael died. There was a period when they used guest singers before signing on to do a reality TV series called Rockstar that ultimately resulted in JD Fortune, a Canadian singer, getting the gig."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring Companion (Late 1980s)
podcast.body: Sinead O'Connor toured with INXS shortly after her debut album was released, with Andy Rourke and Mike Joyce of The Smiths providing her rhythm section. "She quickly found herself on tour with inexess and David Bowie with Andy Warken, Mike Joyce, the rhythm section of the Smiths in her band."
